Title: Table Balance and the New Banned List

Messages.Author: Eric Simon
Messages.Body:
I'm starting a new thread because I know the announcement thread is
just going to keep filling up with both complaints and praise, and I
want to take the discussion in another (less argumentative) direction.

I'm also thinking about a reason given by LSJ on the Conclave list and
bringing it here because that's not the place for ongoing discussion.
Specifically, he said that DU and KR violate the fundamental structure
of the game: the predator/prey relationship. Now in my mind, V:TES is
about much more than this relationship - it has always been and will
continue to be a game about table balance because of its multi-player
nature. Table balance as a game structure does not go away because of
the banning of table-switch cards, but it does change SIGNIFICANTLY
(or at least I think so). So I want to hear discussion about how
table-balancing strategy changes.

Here are some initial thoughts to spark discussion:

In a 5-player game, if you can survive and oust your prey before time,
you can still come in 2nd as opposed to 1st, but there are now fewer
ways for this to happen. A 3/2 split only occurs if you allow your
prey to run away with the table (and if you do, you're not likely to
split 3/2), and there are just a couple of ways to end up with 1.5
while someone else has 2 or 2.5. How much less will people worry
about really strong decks across the table? Does deal-making become
more formulaic? (e.g. - always favoring your grandpredator over your
grandprey because of the point spread)

Because of the more pressing need to specifically slow down your prey
more than you slow down others, I wonder if we'll see a resurgence in
Life Boon. And perhaps this even makes Extremis Boon a more viable
prayer card. Or does it? Were those cards more often tied to
table-switching?

Does this update redeem or make worse some of the classic "bad play"
styles (such as irresponsible bleed)? I can see arguments both ways,
so I'm curious what others think.

What are some of the other strategies that change or improve because
of this new environment?

Eric Simon
Prince of Chicago

vol...@yahoo.com (Eric Simon) wrote in message news:<6f81fa2c.04120...@posting.google.com>...

> What are some of the other strategies that change or improve because
> of this new environment?

One of the most significant random factors in V:tES is table seating.
Good or bad seating often decides a game, and with the exception of
the final round of a tournament, players now have no control over it.

I know that a lot of top-notch tourney players liked to include
table-switching votes as a way of reducing the impact of this random
factor. Perhaps we'll see more toolbox decks played now, since those
decks seem to be less affected by seating than focused decks.

I actually think you're addressing the critical issue quite
reasonably. When I posted, I had a sense that we would be seeing
exactly this kind of concern - that removing seat-switch takes away
from the need to table balance. Myself, I'm not sure it does. The
game win conditions still require you to make sure no one else is
running away with the table, and ideally that you're setting
everything up for a sweep. Perhaps Kindred Spirits becomes less
important as a balancing tool because you're not really going to take
DIRECT advantage of someone else's pool loss, but it can still be an
excellent carrot or stick to try to set the table up for yourself.

I think what I'm getting at here is that a lot of what we've seen in
the past has been OFFENSIVE table balance. This can still be useful
in keeping an individual deck from overpowering everyone. However,
maybe what we'll start to see now is more DEFENSIVE table balance,
such as boons.

I'm not sure, of course, and I think it'll take time to see how this
affects play, but this is certainly a possibility.

'Cause using Bum's Rush and Kindred Spirits cross table DOESN'T MAKE YOU
WIN. In fact, it usually makes you not win. Cross table shenanigins, like
Rushing or KRCing or Kindred Spiriting the guy across the table usually:

A) Weakens your own position, as you are using your resources and actions to
negatively effect someone who is not directly related to you via standard
table relationships.

B) Strengthens someone elses position, as you are harming their predator or
prey.

Yes, yes. Sometimes, due to table politics or whatever, that cross table
Rush/KRC/Whatever does the exact right thing and wins you the game. But
usually this just isn't going to happen. As a result, there is built in
disincentive to partake in cross table shenanigins. It is usually a bad idea
to Rush cross table. That is what prevents people from doing it (assuimg
that they are interested in winning the game, as opposed to, like, just
screwing around and pissing off their friends).

(as opposed to, say, a cross table Rush) result in someone doing something
specifically related to winning the game and specifically strengthening
their position--it steals a VP (specifically getting you closer to winning
the game) and gets you 6 pool (strengthening your position), by switching
seats and VP sniping.

Do you see where the difference lies?

A) Cross table Rush. Usually not a good idea. Usually weakens your position.
Usually strengthens someone elses position. Usually works *against* you
actually winning the game.

B) Cross table VP sniping. Usually a good idea. Usually strengthens your
position. Usually works directly in favor of you winning the game.

This strikes me as incredibly easy to differentiate. Can we move past the
faulty comparisions between DU and a Bum's Rush? I mean, yeah, ok, I can see
people argiung that table switch votes weren't a problem and shouldn't have
been banned for whatever reason, but trying to draw a parallel between DU

For a while, a lot of the vote decks generated from "Ooh, I can switch
the tables around when I do badly against my prey" vote decks will
disappear. Just as any "Oooh, that's shiny" tends to attract magpies, I
believe that a number have been attracted to such simply for that.[0]

So in some circles, vote decks may well become relegated to a few
players trying them every now and then, or whatever. At least for a
while, and assuming that KMW doesn't bring its own magpie cards. In
such circles, this may allow for some kick-ass vote decks to be formed
when they suddenly find that "everyone" has dumped their DTs and so on.

The decks that are left will have to up their game somewhat - they can't
rely on a "lucky"[1] vote pass putting them into a good position.

*extremely* powerful votes left. Voting also has some significant pool-
gain options. Okay, pool gain/bloat isn't as sexy as uber-damage and
table-switching but it's still very useful. Rumors of Gehenna still has
a lot of mileage - even if a number of its primary uses are
trick/master-heavy decks, or subsumed by (say) Anson.

Brinksmanship seems to have its fans - though it's not a card I
personally like, as I think I've mentioned before. (I believe - like
the predator/prey relationship - that the push/pull of pool/defence was
also a fundamental facet of the game.)

For specific decks (hybrid vote/rush, usually) there are things like
Alastor, Templar and Archon have uses, as does Anathema.

The First Tradition used to be quite popular, but its time seems to have
passed. I'd quite like to see it come back.

And there are a random assortment of other vote cards that are still
usable in lots of decks, even if not "primary" cards. (Cue someone
saying "But you missed out how useful Regaining the Upper Hand is in
this deck! How could you?")

I don't think vote is dead by any stretch. It will go into a lull in
places, but I think this will discourage some of the players who were
really only playing it for Dramatic Upheaval's power.
